name: Battle of Salamis
info: An Allied Greek fleet under Themistocles defeated a larger Achaemenid fleet under King Xerxes in the straits between the island of Salamis and the mainland in 480 BCE, after which Xerxes withdrew with much of his army.

facts.date: 480 BCE; no day is stated, and the timeline of the battle is difficult to establish with certainty
facts.place: The straits between the island of Salamis and the mainland, in the Saronic Gulf near Athens, Greece
facts.sides: The Allied Greek city-states, nominally under the Spartan Eurybiades and effectively under the Athenian Themistocles, with 378 triremes by Herodotus's count (his contingents add up to 371), 310 by Aeschylus and 220 by Hyperides; the Achaemenid Empire under King Xerxes, with 1,207 triremes at the outset by Herodotus, though most modern historians favour 600 to 800 at Salamis
facts.outcome: A Greek victory. The Persian fleet withdrew to Phalerum, its losses unstated by Herodotus and estimated at 200 to 300 ships from his later figures, and Xerxes retreated to Asia with much of his army, leaving Mardonius in Greece.

t: Herodotus gives the Persian fleet 1,207 triremes at the outset, but some modern historians say no more than around 600 could have been launched into the Aegean, and most favour 600 to 800 at Salamis itself.

In the cramped straits the great Persian numbers hindered the fleet, as ships struggled to manoeuvre and became disorganised, and the Persians were drawn in partly by a message Themistocles sent to Xerxes.
After Salamis the Peloponnese was safe from conquest and the Persians were dealt a blow to their prestige; the following year the remaining Persian army lost at Plataea and the fleet at Mycale.
dyk: Xerxes had a throne set up on the slopes of Mount Aigaleo, overlooking the straits, so that he could watch the battle and record the names of commanders who performed particularly well.
ev: Darius sends emissaries asking for earth and water; Athens puts the ambassadors on trial and executes them, and Sparta throws them down a well
A heavily outnumbered Athenian army defeats the Persian force at Marathon
Athens, under the guidance of Themistocles, decides to build a massive fleet of triremes
A congress of city-states at Corinth forms a confederate alliance of Greeks
The Greeks hold Thermopylae for three days and fight at Artemisium, then the Allied fleet withdraws to Salamis and the Persians take Attica

The Greek fleet defeats the Persian fleet in the straits of Salamis

sections.background:
The Greek city-states of Athens and Eretria had supported the Ionian Revolt against the Persian Empire of Darius I in 499 to 494 BCE, and Darius vowed to punish those involved. In 491 BCE he sent emissaries to the Greek cities asking for earth and water as a token of submission. Most obliged, but in Athens the ambassadors were put on trial and executed, and in Sparta they were thrown down a well. In 490 BCE a force under Datis and Artaphernes destroyed Eretria and landed at Marathon, where a heavily outnumbered Athenian army won and the Persians withdrew to Asia.

Darius began raising a huge new army, but an Egyptian revolt in 486 BCE postponed it, and he died while preparing to march on Egypt. His son Xerxes I crushed the revolt and restarted the preparations, which included bridging the Hellespont and digging a canal across the isthmus of Mount Athos. In Athens the decision of 482 BCE, under the guidance of Themistocles, was to build a massive fleet of triremes. A congress of city-states met at Corinth in late autumn 481 BCE and formed a confederate alliance, remarkable in a Greek world where many members were still technically at war with each other.

The allies first meant to hold the Vale of Tempe but withdrew, then adopted a dual strategy: the pass of Thermopylae would be blocked on land and the straits of Artemisium by sea. The Spartan king Leonidas held Thermopylae for three days before being outflanked by a mountain path, and the Spartans and Thespians who stayed were surrounded and killed. The fighting at Artemisium had been a stalemate, and the Allied fleet withdrew when news of Thermopylae arrived.
sections.forces:
Herodotus reports 378 triremes in the Allied fleet, but his figures for the contingents add up to 371. The difference may be a garrison of 12 ships left at Aegina, and he says two ships defected from the Persians, so the total at Salamis would be 373 or 380. Aeschylus, who fought at Salamis, gives 310 triremes. Ctesias claims the Athenians had only 110, which ties in with Aeschylus, and Hyperides gives 220 for the whole fleet. Themistocles effectively commanded, but the Spartan nobleman Eurybiades was nominal leader, a compromise after the other states with navies objected to Themistocles claiming leadership.

For the Persians, Herodotus gives 1,207 triremes at the outset. By his reckoning about a third were lost in a storm off Magnesia, 200 more off Euboea and at least 50 at Artemisium; he says the losses were replaced but names only 120 ships from the Greeks of Thrace and nearby islands. Aeschylus also gives 1,207, Diodorus and Lysias 1,200 at Doriskos, Isocrates 1,300 at Doriskos and 1,200 at Salamis, and Ctesias 1,000. Some modern historians accept 1,207 for the initial fleet, while others say the Persians could have launched no more than around 600 warships. Very few accept that many at Salamis: most favour 600 to 800.

Herodotus describes the Persian ships as having better sailing, probably owing to superior seamanship, while most Athenian ships were newly built and had inexperienced crews. He suggests the Allied ships were heavier, perhaps because of fully armoured hoplite marines. The Persians and Asiatic Greeks used a manoeuvre called the diekplous, probably rowing into gaps between ships and ramming them in the side, and the Allies developed tactics to counter it.
sections.course:
In the Allied fleet the Athenians were on the left and probably the Spartans on the right, though Diodorus says it was the Megareans and Aeginetans, with the other contingents in the centre. The Persian fleet was sent to block the exit from the straits the evening before. Herodotus believed it entered the straits at nightfall, but modern historians have debated this, some pointing to the difficulty of manoeuvring in a confined space by night. Aeschylus gives the Persians three ranks, with the Phoenicians on the right next to Mount Aigaleo and the Ionians on the left. About 400 troops were placed on the island of Psyttaleia, and Diodorus adds that the Egyptian fleet was sent round Salamis to block the northern exit, which Herodotus does not mention.

The Persians did not attack until daylight. Aeschylus says that as they approached they heard the Greeks singing their battle hymn. The Allies at first appeared to back their ships away, which Plutarch says was to gain better position and to wait for the early morning wind. Herodotus recounts that a single ship then shot forward to ram the nearest Persian vessel; the Athenians claimed it was the ship of Ameinias of Pallene, the Aeginetans one of theirs. The whole Greek line followed.

As the first Persian line was pushed back it fouled the second and third lines. On the Greek left the Persian admiral Ariabignes, a brother of Xerxes, was killed early, and the leaderless Phoenician squadrons appear to have been pushed against the coast, many vessels running aground. In the centre a wedge of Greek ships split the Persian fleet in two. The Persians began to retreat towards Phalerum, and Herodotus says the Aeginetans ambushed them as they tried to leave the straits.
sections.aftermath:
Herodotus does not give the Persian losses, but he writes that the next year the Persian fleet numbered 300 triremes. The number lost therefore depends on the size of the fleet at the start; something in the range of 200 to 300 seems likely on the estimates above. Herodotus says the Persians suffered many more casualties than the Greeks because most of them did not know how to swim. The Athenian general Aristides took a detachment across to Psyttaleia and killed the garrison Xerxes had left there. Herodotus says Xerxes had Phoenician captains beheaded for blaming the Ionians for cowardice; Diodorus says he put to death the Phoenicians chiefly responsible for the flight, and that the Phoenicians sailed to Asia that night.

Xerxes tried to build a pontoon bridge or causeway across the straits to attack the Athenians, but with the Greek fleet patrolling the straits it proved futile. At a council of war Mardonius, according to Herodotus, offered to attack the Peloponnese or, if the king was resolved to withdraw, to remain and conquer Greece with 300,000 chosen troops. Fearing that the Greeks might attack the bridges over the Hellespont and trap his army in Europe, Xerxes took the greater part of the army home. Mardonius picked the troops who stayed, the elite infantry and cavalry. The Persians left Attica, Mardonius wintered in Boeotia and Thessaly, and the Athenians returned to their burnt city.

In 479 BCE Mardonius recaptured Athens, and the Allies under Spartan leadership marched on Attica. The two armies met near Plataea, where the Greeks won, destroying much of the Persian army. At the near-simultaneous Battle of Mycale the Allied fleet destroyed much of the remaining Persian fleet.
sections.sources:
The battle is not well described by ancient sources, and it is unlikely that anyone other than perhaps Xerxes had a clear idea what was happening across the width of the straits. Herodotus is the main narrator, and the playwright Aeschylus, who fought at Salamis, also gives details and figures. Plutarch, Diodorus, Ctesias and Hyperides supply further claims, and they often disagree. What can be written is more of a discussion than a definitive account.

The timeline is difficult to establish. Herodotus presents the battle as though it occurred directly after the capture of Athens but nowhere says so explicitly, and it is more likely that the Persians spent two or three weeks capturing Athens, refitting and resupplying. It is also hard to explain exactly what brought about the battle. The rift among the Allies that reached Xerxes may have been a ruse, or a response to Persian offensive manoeuvres, and the Peloponnesians may have been party to the stratagem of Themistocles, so calmly did they accept that they must fight. Whether the Persians entered the straits at night or at dawn is debated. The Athenian story that the Corinthians sailed away at the start was denied by all the other Greeks, and the Athenians and Aeginetans each claimed the first ramming. The Persian losses and the size of both fleets depend on figures that the sources do not agree on.

On 17 March 2017 archaeologists announced that they had uncovered the partially submerged remains of the anchorage used by the Greek warships before the battle, at the Ambelaki-Kynosaurus site on the island of Salamis.
sections.legacy:
Salamis marked the turning point of the Greco-Persian wars. After it the Peloponnese, and by extension Greece as an entity, was safe from conquest, and the Persians suffered a major blow to their prestige and morale as well as severe material losses. After Plataea and Mycale the threat of conquest was removed and the Allies could go on the counter-offensive. The Greek victory allowed Macedon to revolt against Persian rule, and over the next 30 years Thrace, the Aegean islands and finally Ionia were removed from Persian control by the Allies or by their Athenian-dominated successor, the Delian League.

Like Marathon and Thermopylae, Salamis has gained something of a legendary status, perhaps because of the desperate circumstances and the unlikely odds. A significant number of historians have called it one of the most significant battles in human history. In a more extreme form of the argument, some historians hold that a Greek defeat would have stifled the growth of Western civilisation, on the premise that philosophy, science, personal freedom and democracy are rooted in the legacy of ancient Greece. The celebrated blossoming of Athenian culture came only after the Persian wars were won.

Militarily it is difficult to draw many lessons from Salamis, because of the uncertainty about what happened. The Allies chose their ground to negate Persian numbers but had to rely on the Persians launching an attack that, by the argument of Artemisia, they did not need to make; perhaps the most important lesson is the deception by Themistocles. According to Plutarch, the previously undistinguished Cimon won great repute among the Athenians for his courage in the battle, which later enabled him to launch his political career.

summary: At Salamis in 480 BCE an Allied Greek fleet under Themistocles fought a larger Persian fleet under Xerxes in the narrow straits off Athens and won, after which Xerxes withdrew with much of his army. The size of both fleets and the Persian losses are disputed.
references: Jeffrey A. Smith, Themistocles: The Powerbroker of Athens (Pen & Sword Military, 2021)
notes: The article gives no day or month for the battle and says the timeline is hard to establish; span is '480 BCE'.

Greek fleet figures differ: Herodotus 378 (contingents sum to 371; 373 or 380 at Salamis), Aeschylus 310, Hyperides 220, Ctesias 110 Athenian. Persian: Herodotus 1,207 initial; modern view 600-800 at Salamis; Persian losses 200-300 'seems likely' is the article's own inference from Herodotus's 300 ships the next year.
Article says the Allied/Persian dispositions differ between Herodotus and Diodorus (north-south vs east-west; Egyptian detachment); both kept, hedged.

Article contradicts itself slightly on the Greek left: 'On the Greek left the Persian admiral Ariabignes was killed ... Phoenician squadrons pushed back against the coast'. Written as the article has it.
The article's phrase 'the high point of the second Persian invasion' and 'arguably the largest naval battle of the ancient world' were left out as hedged claims not needed.

Left out: Themistocles's inscriptions to the Ionians, Artemisia's ramming of the Calyndian ship, the apparition of a woman, Plutarch's account of Ariabignes's death, Aeschylus's paean text, the Athenian 'Aristides arrives' detail, the lesson about Marathon's comparison. Aristides's role on Psyttaleia: article says 'slaughter the garrison'; written as 'killed'.
The 'Egyptian' claim in aftermath and the 'whether Persians knew to swim' claim are Herodotus's, attributed.
